label: Synthesis with Yosys and ABC
lesson:
# Synthesis with Yosys and ABC

The standard open-source synthesis flow is Yosys for the front end and word-level optimization and ABC for combinational logic optimization and mapping. Yosys reads Verilog into its RTLIL representation, lowers processes, optimizes, maps memories and arithmetic, and hands each combinational region to ABC. Knowing what each pass does lets a tool designer place a new optimization where its information still exists.

## Front end and process lowering

Yosys parses Verilog into an abstract syntax tree and elaborates it into RTLIL: modules, wires and cells, plus processes for always blocks. The proc family turns processes into netlist cells: decision trees become multiplexers, clocked assignments become flip-flop cells (with asynchronous reset where present), and incompletely assigned combinational variables become latches. The opt family then simplifies: opt_expr folds constants, opt_merge merges identical cells, opt_muxtree removes unreachable multiplexer branches, and opt_clean deletes unused cells and wires. At this point the design is still word-level, which is where fsm extraction, memory inference and arithmetic grouping (alumacc, share) work.

## Lowering and the hand-off to ABC

techmap replaces word-level cells such as adders, comparators and multipliers with implementations from a map library, ending in Yosys's internal single-bit gates (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, MUX cell types). Flip-flops are mapped to library cells by dfflibmap with a Liberty file. The abc pass then extracts the combinational logic between registers, writes it to ABC, runs an ABC script (strash, rewriting and balancing passes, then mapping to the Liberty cells or to LUTs) and reads the mapped netlist back. Because ABC sees only combinational logic, registers are handled separately, and anything not exported to ABC, such as keep-marked nets, survives as is.

## Where new optimizations belong

Each representation keeps different information. Recognizing a special multiplier, re-encoding an FSM, or sharing an adder between exclusive branches needs word-level RTLIL, before techmap bit-blasts it. Generic Boolean optimization belongs in ABC on the AIG. Library-aware sizing belongs after mapping. FPGA scripts (for example synth_ice40) replace the Liberty mapping with LUT mapping and techmap to device primitives such as carry chains and block RAMs. When QoR changes between versions, the ABC script and ABC version used inside the abc pass are the usual cause, since most combinational optimization happens there.

## Going deeper

Wolf, Glaser and Kepler, "Yosys: a free Verilog synthesis suite", Austrochip (2013); Brayton and Mishchenko, "ABC: an academic industrial-strength verification tool", CAV (2010); the Yosys manual.

problems.q:
What does the opt family of Yosys passes do?

A) Constant folding, merging identical cells, simplifying mux trees and removing unused cells and wires

B) Extracts finite state machines and recodes them

C) Maps cells to a Liberty library

D) Places the cells
problems.a: Constant folding, merging identical cells, simplifying mux trees and removing unused cells and wires
problems.e: opt runs subpasses such as opt_expr, opt_merge, opt_muxtree and opt_clean until nothing changes.

problems.q:
Which Yosys pass turns always blocks (processes) into multiplexers and flip-flop cells?

A) proc

B) opt

C) abc

D) techmap
problems.a: proc
problems.e: proc lowers RTLIL processes into netlist cells: multiplexers for the decision trees and dff or adff cells for clocked assignments.

problems.q:
In a Yosys standard-cell flow, what does the abc pass do?

A) Exports the combinational logic to ABC, which optimizes it and maps it to the given library, then reads the result back

B) Converts processes to netlists

C) Removes hierarchy

D) Maps flip-flops to library cells
problems.a: Exports the combinational logic to ABC, which optimizes it and maps it to the given library, then reads the result back
problems.e: abc handles combinational logic; flip-flops are mapped separately, for example with dfflibmap.

problems.q:
After techmap but before abc, a Yosys netlist is full of cells of type _AND_, _OR_ and _NOT_. What are they?

A) Placement blockages

B) Library cells from the Liberty file

C) ABC script commands

D) Yosys internal single-bit gate cells, still technology independent
problems.a: Yosys internal single-bit gate cells, still technology independent
problems.e: techmap lowers to Yosys's own gate library; only abc and dfflibmap bind to a real library.

problems.q:
What does the Yosys fsm pass do?

A) Minimizes every register in the design

B) Removes all state machines

C) Converts FSMs into ROMs

D) Detects state registers, extracts the FSM, optimizes it and re-encodes the states
problems.a: Detects state registers, extracts the FSM, optimizes it and re-encodes the states
problems.e: fsm finds registers that behave as state, builds an fsm cell, optimizes it and maps it back with a new encoding.

problems.q:
Why does Yosys run alumacc and share before techmap?

A) To group arithmetic into alu and macc cells and to share resources while they are still word-level

B) To map flip-flops to the library

C) To flatten the hierarchy

D) To compute timing
problems.a: To group arithmetic into alu and macc cells and to share resources while they are still word-level
problems.e: Word-level views make arithmetic sharing and macro recognition possible; after bit-blasting these opportunities are hard to see.

problems.q:
Why does Yosys keep RTLIL as an intermediate representation rather than lowering straight to gates?

A) RTLIL stores placement information

B) RTLIL is faster to simulate than gates

C) Word-level cells keep structure that passes such as fsm, memory, share and alumacc need

D) ABC cannot read gate-level netlists
problems.a: Word-level cells keep structure that passes such as fsm, memory, share and alumacc need
problems.e: Lowering early destroys the information those passes exploit.

problems.q:
Synthesis results change between two Yosys versions on the same RTL. Which component most often explains it?

A) The hierarchy check

B) The order of ports in the module

C) The Verilog parser's handling of comments

D) The ABC script and ABC version used inside the abc pass
problems.a: The ABC script and ABC version used inside the abc pass
problems.e: Most combinational QoR comes from ABC, and its default scripts and heuristics evolve.

problems.q:
A Yosys flow for an FPGA runs synth_ice40 or a similar script. What changes compared with a standard-cell flow?

A) proc is skipped

B) Logic is mapped to LUTs and vendor primitives instead of a Liberty library

C) Flip-flops are removed

D) The abc pass is replaced by placement
problems.a: Logic is mapped to LUTs and vendor primitives instead of a Liberty library
problems.e: FPGA scripts call ABC in LUT-mapping mode and techmap to device primitives such as carry chains and block RAMs.

label: ABC optimization scripts
lesson:
# ABC optimization scripts

ABC exposes its transformations as commands and combines them into scripts. resyn, resyn2 and compress2 are the classic recipes: sequences of balancing, rewriting and refactoring that each improve the AIG a little and set up the next pass. A script is a strategy in the engine's four-layer sense, and choosing or learning scripts is a natural job for an agent.

## The core commands

strash builds a structurally hashed AIG from the current network. balance (b) rebuilds AND supergates for minimum depth. rewrite (rw) replaces 4-input cuts by better precomputed structures. refactor (rf) collapses larger cuts and re-factors them. resub (rs) re-expresses nodes using existing divisors. The z variants, rwz and rfz, also accept zero-gain moves. fraig merges functionally equivalent nodes found by simulation and SAT. For mapping, map targets a standard-cell library and if maps to K-input LUTs. cec proves combinational equivalence of two networks. Each command preserves function; they differ in what they optimize and how much they cost.

## Reading resyn2

resyn2 is b; rw; rf; b; rw; rwz; b; rfz; rwz; b. It alternates area moves (rewrite and refactor) with depth moves (balance), and ends with zero-cost variants that reshape the graph so later passes, or a second run, find more gains. Each pass is greedy and local, so running resyn2 twice usually helps a little more. compress2 is the same pattern with the -l option on each command, preserving logic levels, for timing-critical designs. dch computes structural choices before mapping, so the mapper can pick among equivalent structures, which reduces the structural bias that any single AIG imposes.

## Scripts as strategy

Script quality depends on the design. Arithmetic-heavy logic responds differently from control logic, and long scripts trade run time for QoR. The commands are compiled, verified transformations; the script is policy that selects and orders them, so changing the script is a configuration or plug-in change, not a core edit. That makes script choice a natural search space: design-space exploration tries variants, and learned policies choose the next command from AIG statistics. Whatever chooses the script, every result must still pass equivalence checking, and proxies such as node count must be confirmed by mapped area and timing.

## Going deeper

Brayton and Mishchenko, "ABC: an academic industrial-strength verification tool", CAV (2010); Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "DAG-aware AIG rewriting", DAC (2006); the ABC command documentation.

problems.q:
In ABC scripts, what do b, rw and rf stand for?

A) bdd, read and reflect

B) bind, rename and resize

C) balance, rewrite and refactor

D) buffer, rewire and refine
problems.a: balance, rewrite and refactor
problems.e: These are the three core AIG transformations; resyn-style scripts interleave them.

problems.q:
In ABC scripts, what do b, rw and rf stand for?

A) bind, rename and resize

B) bdd, read and reflect

C) balance, rewrite and refactor

D) buffer, rewire and refine
problems.a: balance, rewrite and refactor
problems.e: These are the three core AIG transformations; resyn-style scripts interleave them.

problems.q:
What does the ABC command strash do?

A) Reads a Liberty library

B) Maps the AIG to LUTs

C) Converts the current network into a structurally hashed AIG

D) Balances the AIG
problems.a: Converts the current network into a structurally hashed AIG
problems.e: strash builds the AIG representation that rewrite, refactor and balance operate on.

problems.q:
Running resyn2 a second time still reduces the AIG a little. Why?

A) resyn2 is randomized

B) The AIG function changed

C) Each pass is greedy and local, so the new structure exposes new opportunities

D) The first run did not finish
problems.a: Each pass is greedy and local, so the new structure exposes new opportunities
problems.e: Iterating heuristic passes continues to improve until a fixpoint, with diminishing returns.

problems.q:
Why do ABC scripts call balance between rewriting passes?

A) Rewriting minimizes nodes and can deepen the graph; balancing restores depth

B) Balance removes redundant nodes

C) Balance is required before every command by ABC's syntax

D) Balance maps the AIG to cells
problems.a: Rewriting minimizes nodes and can deepen the graph; balancing restores depth
problems.e: Interleaving trades area-driven moves against depth-driven ones.

problems.q:
Which ABC command maps an AIG into K-input LUTs?

A) strash -K 6

B) map -K 6

C) if -K 6

D) balance -K 6
problems.a: if -K 6
problems.e: if is ABC's cut-based mapper; -K sets the LUT size. map is the standard-cell mapper.

problems.q:
A user's ABC script runs fraig before rewriting. What does it gain?

A) It computes timing

B) It maps the design faster

C) It removes all registers

D) Functionally equivalent nodes are merged first, so rewriting starts from a smaller, redundancy-free AIG
problems.a: Functionally equivalent nodes are merged first, so rewriting starts from a smaller, redundancy-free AIG
problems.e: FRAIGing merges equivalent nodes found by simulation and SAT, which plain structural hashing misses.

problems.q:
Which ABC command checks combinational equivalence of two networks?

A) resyn2

B) if

C) sweep

D) cec
problems.a: cec
problems.e: cec builds a miter and proves it unsatisfiable with simulation, FRAIGing and SAT.

problems.q:
A script runs rw several times and the AIG node count stops changing, yet the mapped area later improves with rwz. Why?

A) Zero-gain moves change structure without changing count, and the new structure maps better

B) rwz changes the function

C) rwz adds don't cares

D) rwz is a mapping command
problems.a: Zero-gain moves change structure without changing count, and the new structure maps better
problems.e: Node count is a proxy; equal-size structures can differ in mappability.

label: Combinational equivalence checking with miters
lesson:
# Combinational equivalence checking with miters

Every synthesis transformation must preserve function, and combinational equivalence checking proves it. The method builds a miter, a circuit that outputs 1 exactly when the two designs disagree, and proves that it can never output 1. Simulation, FRAIG-style sweeping and SAT make this scale to large designs, and it is the golden test for any new optimization.

## The miter

Given two circuits with matching inputs and outputs, connect corresponding inputs, XOR each pair of corresponding outputs, and OR the XORs together. The miter output is 1 on an input vector exactly when some output pair differs there. The designs are equivalent if and only if the miter is unsatisfiable. For $F = a(\bar{b} + \bar{c})$ and a rewrite $G = a(\bar{b} + \bar{b})$, the miter is 1 where they differ: with $a = 1$, $b = 0$ both are 1, with $b = 1$, $c = 0$ only $F$ is 1. Counting such vectors over the free inputs gives the number of counterexamples.

## Several outputs

For a multi-output circuit the miter ORs the per-output XORs, so a vector is a counterexample if any output differs. The counterexample count is the size of the union of the per-output difference sets, not their sum: two outputs that each differ on 4 vectors, 2 of them shared, give 6 counterexamples. In practice the checker does not count; it stops at the first satisfying assignment and reports it as a counterexample, which is often simulated to locate the bug. Checking outputs one at a time gives smaller SAT problems and points directly at the failing output.

## Making the proof scale

The miter of two cones with $A$ and $B$ AND nodes has about $A + B$ nodes plus three per output XOR and one per OR, so two outputs add 7. Solving it directly with SAT is hard when the two designs are structurally different. Real checkers first structurally hash the miter, which merges identical logic, then simulate to find candidate internal equivalences, prove them with SAT from the inputs upward (SAT sweeping), and merge them. Once internal points match, the output XORs often collapse to constant 0. ABC's cec command implements this. Retiming breaks register correspondence, so sequential transformations need sequential equivalence checking instead.

## Going deeper

Kuehlmann, Paruthi, Krohm and Ganai, "Robust Boolean reasoning for equivalence checking and functional property verification", IEEE TCAD (2002); Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton and Een, "Improvements to combinational equivalence checking", ICCAD (2006).

problems.q: An optimizer rewrote $F = (c \oplus (b \cdot \overline{a})) \cdot c$ into $G = c \cdot b \cdot \overline{a} \cdot c$ over inputs a, b, c. Build the miter $F \oplus G$. How many input vectors set the miter output to 1? (0 means the rewrite is correct.)
problems.e: The miter is 1 exactly where F and G differ. Comparing truth tables gives 4 such vectors.

problems.q: An optimizer rewrote $F = a + ((c + \overline{d}) \cdot (b + \overline{a}))$ into $G = a + ((c + \overline{d}) \cdot b \cdot \overline{a})$ over inputs a, b, c, d. Build the miter $F \oplus G$. How many input vectors set the miter output to 1? (0 means the rewrite is correct.)
problems.e: The miter is 1 exactly where F and G differ. Comparing truth tables gives 3 such vectors.

problems.q: An optimizer rewrote $F = (\overline{d} + (\overline{b} \oplus c) + a) \cdot d$ into $G = (d + (\overline{b} \oplus c) + a) \cdot d$ over inputs a, b, c, d. Build the miter $F \oplus G$. How many input vectors set the miter output to 1? (0 means the rewrite is correct.)
problems.e: The miter is 1 exactly where F and G differ. Comparing truth tables gives 2 such vectors.

problems.q: A two-output circuit computes $F_1 = (a \cdot c) + (\overline{b} \cdot (a \oplus c))$ and $F_2 = b + (c \cdot \overline{a})$; the optimized version computes $G_1 = (a \cdot c) + (\overline{b} \cdot (a \oplus c))$ and $G_2 = b + (c \cdot a)$. The miter ORs the XORs of corresponding outputs. On how many input vectors is the miter 1?
problems.e: A vector is a counterexample if any output pair differs. 2 vectors are.

problems.q: A two-output circuit computes $F_1 = (d + a + b) \oplus c \oplus d$ and $F_2 = a + \overline{b} + c$; the optimized version computes $G_1 = (d + a + b) \oplus a \oplus d$ and $G_2 = c + \overline{b} + c$. The miter ORs the XORs of corresponding outputs. On how many input vectors is the miter 1?
problems.e: A vector is a counterexample if any output pair differs. 8 vectors are.

problems.q: A two-output circuit computes $F_1 = \overline{b} \cdot (a + \overline{c})$ and $F_2 = c + (((b \oplus a) + c) \oplus \overline{b})$; the optimized version computes $G_1 = \overline{b} \cdot (a + c)$ and $G_2 = \overline{\overline{c} \cdot \overline{((b \oplus a) + c) \oplus \overline{b}}}$. The miter ORs the XORs of corresponding outputs. On how many input vectors is the miter 1?
problems.e: A vector is a counterexample if any output pair differs. 2 vectors are.

problems.q: Build the AIG miter of a two-output circuit, $F_1 = (b \oplus c) + (a \cdot \overline{b})$, $F_2 = b \cdot a \cdot c$, against its rewrite, $G_1 = (b \oplus c) + (a \cdot b)$, $G_2 = b \cdot a \cdot b$, with no structural sharing. Each two-input AND or OR is one AND node, an XOR is three, and the final OR of the two output XORs is one. How many AND nodes does the miter have?
problems.e: The four cones cost 5, 2, 5 and 2 AND nodes; two output XORs cost 6 and the OR costs 1. Total 21.

problems.q: Build the AIG miter of a two-output circuit, $F_1 = (a + \overline{c}) \cdot b \cdot a$, $F_2 = \overline{c} \oplus (b \cdot a)$, against its rewrite, $G_1 = (a + \overline{c}) \cdot b \cdot a$, $G_2 = \overline{c} \oplus (b \cdot a)$, with no structural sharing. Each two-input AND or OR is one AND node, an XOR is three, and the final OR of the two output XORs is one. How many AND nodes does the miter have?
problems.e: The four cones cost 3, 4, 3 and 4 AND nodes; two output XORs cost 6 and the OR costs 1. Total 21.

problems.q: Build the AIG miter of a two-output circuit, $F_1 = a \cdot (c + \overline{b})$, $F_2 = (a \oplus b) + c$, against its rewrite, $G_1 = c \cdot (c + \overline{b})$, $G_2 = (a \cdot b) + c$, with no structural sharing. Each two-input AND or OR is one AND node, an XOR is three, and the final OR of the two output XORs is one. How many AND nodes does the miter have?
problems.e: The four cones cost 2, 4, 2 and 2 AND nodes; two output XORs cost 6 and the OR costs 1. Total 17.

label: Learning synthesis recipes
lesson:
# Learning synthesis recipes

The order of ABC commands matters, and the best script depends on the design. That makes recipe selection a sequential decision problem: an agent observes the AIG, picks the next command, and receives a reward computed by the tools. Framed carefully, it is a clean case of tool-grounded reinforcement learning; framed carelessly, it rewards gaming a proxy.

## A tool-grounded reward

The reward comes from the tools, not from a model's opinion. A simple one weighs area and depth against a baseline: $R = w \frac{A_0 - A}{A_0} + (1 - w) \frac{L_0 - L}{L_0}$, with $A$ the AND count and $L$ the level count after the recipe, and $A_0$, $L_0$ the baseline. With $A_0 = 1753$, $L_0 = 39$ and $w = 0.5$, a recipe reaching 1412 nodes and 27 levels earns $0.5 \cdot 0.195 + 0.5 \cdot 0.308 = 0.251$. The weight decides whether area or depth wins. Better rewards use mapped area and delay from the mapper and timer, which cost more to compute but are what users care about.

## State, actions and policy

The state is a summary of the current AIG: node count, levels, balance statistics, and the recent command history. The actions are ABC commands (or short macro sequences). A policy maps state to the next command, trained by policy-gradient or actor-critic methods over many designs, with the episode ending after a fixed number of steps. Closed-loop policies, which observe the AIG after each command, can react to the actual effect of each pass, while open-loop scripts commit in advance. Held-out designs test whether the policy generalizes rather than memorizing what works on the training circuits.

## Where it fits and how it fails

In the four-layer model the learned policy is strategy: it orders compiled, verified transformations and never touches the AIG core, so a bad policy can waste time but cannot break correctness, provided every result passes equivalence checking. The main failure is reward hacking: if the reward is AIG node count, the agent may learn long tails of zero-cost moves or structures that count well but map badly. The defenses are to compute the reward from mapped QoR at least on a schedule, to penalize run time, and to report mapped area, delay, run time and equivalence for every adopted recipe.

## Going deeper

Hosny, Hashemi, Shalan and Reda, "DRiLLS: deep reinforcement learning for logic synthesis", ASP-DAC (2020); Sutton and Barto, "Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction" (2nd ed., 2018), on policy gradients.

problems.q:
An agent learns ABC recipes with the reward $R = 0.5 \cdot \frac{A_0 - A}{A_0} + 0.5 \cdot \frac{L_0 - L}{L_0}$, where the baseline AIG has $A_0 = 1444$ nodes and $L_0 = 22$ levels. On this design, [b; rw; rwz; b; rwz; b] gives 1114 AND nodes and 18 levels; [b -l; rw -l; rf -l; b -l] gives 1281 AND nodes and 15 levels; [rs; rw; rs; rf; b] gives 1200 AND nodes and 18 levels; [fraig; rw; rf; b] gives 1221 AND nodes and 22 levels. Which recipe earns the highest reward?

A) b; rw; rwz; b; rwz; b

B) rs; rw; rs; rf; b

C) fraig; rw; rf; b

D) b -l; rw -l; rf -l; b -l
problems.a: b -l; rw -l; rf -l; b -l
problems.e: Rewards: best 0.216 for [b -l; rw -l; rf -l; b -l], next 0.205. The weighting decides whether area or depth wins; neither is mapped QoR.

problems.q:

On this design, [fraig; rw; rf; b] gives 1458 AND nodes and 34 levels; [b; rw; rwz; b; rwz; b] gives 1492 AND nodes and 35 levels; [rs; rw; rs; rf; b] gives 1541 AND nodes and 26 levels; [b -l; rw -l; rf -l; b -l] gives 1546 AND nodes and 29 levels. B) rs; rw; rs; rf; b

C) fraig; rw; rf; b

D) b; rw; rwz; b; rwz; b

problems.e: Rewards: best 0.190 for [rs; rw; rs; rf; b], next 0.164. The weighting decides whether area or depth wins; neither is mapped QoR.

An agent learns ABC recipes with the reward $R = 0.5 \cdot \frac{A_0 - A}{A_0} + 0.5 \cdot \frac{L_0 - L}{L_0}$, where the baseline AIG has $A_0 = 1848$ nodes and $L_0 = 22$ levels. Which recipe earns the highest reward?

problems.e: Rewards: best 0.257 for [b -l; rw -l; rf -l; b -l], next 0.162. The weighting decides whether area or depth wins; neither is mapped QoR.

problems.q:
Why is a learned recipe policy validated on held-out designs?

A) Because held-out designs have no AND nodes

B) Because training designs cannot be mapped

D) To check that it generalizes rather than memorizing what works on the training circuits
problems.a: To check that it generalizes rather than memorizing what works on the training circuits
problems.e: Recipe quality is design-dependent; overfitting to a benchmark suite is a common failure.

problems.q:
Why is a learned recipe policy validated on held-out designs?

A) To check that it generalizes rather than memorizing what works on the training circuits

B) Because ABC runs faster on new designs

C) Because training designs cannot be mapped

D) Because held-out designs have no AND nodes
problems.a: To check that it generalizes rather than memorizing what works on the training circuits
problems.e: Recipe quality is design-dependent; overfitting to a benchmark suite is a common failure.

problems.q:
The reward is the AIG node reduction after each step. The agent learns to end every episode with many rwz commands. What is the concern?

A) rwz always increases the node count

B) It may be exploiting the proxy: zero-gain moves cost run time and need not improve mapped QoR

C) rwz is not a valid ABC command

D) The agent has found the global optimum
problems.a: It may be exploiting the proxy: zero-gain moves cost run time and need not improve mapped QoR
problems.e: Reward on a fast proxy can be gamed; the real target is mapped area and delay after timing.

problems.q:
Two recipes tie on the training reward. One takes 3 seconds and the other 40. What should the reward design include?

A) A random tie-breaker only

B) Nothing, run time is irrelevant to synthesis

C) A run-time penalty, since the loop and the user pay for every command

D) A bonus for longer scripts
problems.a: A run-time penalty, since the loop and the user pay for every command
problems.e: Practical recipe search optimizes QoR per unit of compute, not QoR alone.

problems.q:
The agent's policy outputs one script per design, chosen before running anything. Why might a closed-loop policy do better?

A) Fixed scripts cannot contain balance

B) ABC runs commands in random order

C) Closed-loop policies never need a reward

D) It observes the AIG after each command and adapts, instead of committing to a fixed sequence
problems.a: It observes the AIG after each command and adapts, instead of committing to a fixed sequence
problems.e: Feedback lets the agent react to the actual effect of each transformation on this design.

problems.q:
Two recipes tie on the training reward. One takes 3 seconds and the other 40. What should the reward design include?

A) A random tie-breaker only

B) A bonus for longer scripts

C) A run-time penalty, since the loop and the user pay for every command

D) Nothing, run time is irrelevant to synthesis
problems.a: A run-time penalty, since the loop and the user pay for every command
problems.e: Practical recipe search optimizes QoR per unit of compute, not QoR alone.

label: Rewrite rule sets as skills
lesson:
# Rewrite rule sets as skills

An equality-saturation engine splits naturally into a fixed core and a variable surface. The core, hashconsing, union-find, rebuild and the extraction interface, guarantees that every represented term is equivalent. Rule sets, schedulers and cost models vary per user. Packaging the variable parts as skills with manifests lets an agent pick and extend them safely.

## Core versus change surface

The immutable core of an e-graph engine is the machinery that makes it correct and fast: hashconsing of e-nodes, union-find over e-classes, congruence rebuild, and the extraction algorithm interface. Rule sets (for adders, multipliers, shifts, a customer's MAC unit), rule schedulers, node and time budgets, and cost models are the change surface. A manifest for a datapath rewriting skill lists the rule sets it supports, the cost models it can extract with, its input and output formats (for example word-level RTLIL or another IR) and its tunable budgets. Raising a node budget is Tier 1, adding a rule set is Tier 2, editing union-find is Tier 3.

## Golden tests for rules

A new rule is promoted only with evidence. Soundness first: both sides must be equal at every bit width and signedness the rule matches, which for small widths can be checked exhaustively and in general with an SMT or bit-vector proof. For example, $x \cdot 2^k \to x \ll k$ holds for two's-complement operands of fixed width, but rules involving division or right shifts need sign conditions. Then equivalence: designs extracted with the rule must pass equivalence checking against their originals. Then a differential QoR report over a benchmark suite shows which designs moved and by how much. Versioning rule sets separately from the engine makes each change traceable and reversible.

## Seams and the flywheel

Two seams carry most customer-specific behavior. The cost seam: the extractor asks, for each e-node, what it costs, given operator, widths and context, so a customer's power or area model plugs in without touching the core. The scheduling seam: a policy decides which rules run when, so explosive rules such as associativity do not exhaust the budget before useful rules fire. A rule set that proves valuable for one design moves through the skill flywheel, iterated as a plug-in, validated by golden and differential tests, then promoted into the shared library with guidance on when to select it. The customer's design stays behind the IP boundary.

## Going deeper

Willsey et al., "egg: fast and extensible equality saturation", POPL (2021), on rule scheduling and extraction; the agent-first engine model in this curriculum's agentic domain.

problems.q:
A team adds a new rewrite rule for their custom multiply-accumulate. Which change tier is that?

A) Tier 2: a plug-in rule set at a defined extension point, with the e-graph core untouched

B) Tier 1: a parameter change

C) Tier 3: an edit to union-find and rebuild

D) Not a change, rules are part of the design
problems.a: Tier 2: a plug-in rule set at a defined extension point, with the e-graph core untouched
problems.e: Rules are policy that the core loads; the saturation and congruence machinery stays fixed.

problems.q:
Which part of an e-graph engine is the immutable core?

A) The particular rule set for adders

B) The node budget

C) Hashconsing, union-find, congruence rebuild and the extraction algorithm interface

D) The cost assigned to a shift
problems.a: Hashconsing, union-find, congruence rebuild and the extraction algorithm interface
problems.e: These guarantee that every represented term is equivalent; rule sets and costs vary per user.

problems.q:
A team adds a new rewrite rule for their custom multiply-accumulate. Which change tier is that?

A) Tier 1: a parameter change

B) Tier 3: an edit to union-find and rebuild

C) Tier 2: a plug-in rule set at a defined extension point, with the e-graph core untouched

D) Not a change, rules are part of the design
problems.a: Tier 2: a plug-in rule set at a defined extension point, with the e-graph core untouched
problems.e: Rules are policy that the core loads; the saturation and congruence machinery stays fixed.

problems.q:
What must the golden test of a new rewrite rule check?

A) That it fires at least once

B) That it keeps the e-graph small

C) That the rule is sound (both sides equal at every bit width it matches) and that designs extracted with it pass equivalence checking

D) That it reduces cost on every design
problems.a: That the rule is sound (both sides equal at every bit width it matches) and that designs extracted with it pass equivalence checking
problems.e: Soundness is the invariant; one unsound rule silently corrupts every term it touches.

problems.q:
Why should rule sets be versioned separately from the e-graph engine?

A) Because the engine changes every run

B) Because versioning makes saturation faster

C) Because rules cannot be compiled

D) So a QoR change can be traced to a rule change and reverted without touching the engine
problems.a: So a QoR change can be traced to a rule change and reverted without touching the engine
problems.e: Separate versions make differential testing and rollback precise.

problems.q:
A differential test runs saturation with and without a new rule on 50 designs. What does it measure?

A) Only that no design failed to parse

B) Only whether the e-graph got larger

C) Which designs' extracted cost changed and by how much, with equivalence confirmed for each

D) Only run time
problems.a: Which designs' extracted cost changed and by how much, with equivalence confirmed for each
problems.e: Differential tests show that only intended designs moved, and only in the intended direction.

problems.q:
Where should an agent's datapath e-graph skill hand results to the rest of the flow?

A) As word-level RTLIL or an equivalent IR before bit-blasting, followed by equivalence checking

B) As placement constraints

C) As a Liberty file

D) As a mapped netlist that skips synthesis
problems.a: As word-level RTLIL or an equivalent IR before bit-blasting, followed by equivalence checking
problems.e: Word-level rewrites belong before lowering; downstream synthesis then optimizes the bits.

problems.q:
Where should an agent's datapath e-graph skill hand results to the rest of the flow?

A) As a Liberty file

B) As a mapped netlist that skips synthesis

C) As word-level RTLIL or an equivalent IR before bit-blasting, followed by equivalence checking

D) As placement constraints
problems.a: As word-level RTLIL or an equivalent IR before bit-blasting, followed by equivalence checking
problems.e: Word-level rewrites belong before lowering; downstream synthesis then optimizes the bits.

problems.q:
The skill flywheel promotes a rule set found for one design into the library. What must stay behind?

A) The manifest

B) The rules themselves

C) The equivalence proofs

D) The customer's design data; only the validated rules and when to use them move into the shared library
problems.a: The customer's design data; only the validated rules and when to use them move into the shared library
problems.e: Know-how flows back to the library; design data stays inside the IP boundary.

label: Equivalence checking as the golden test
lesson:
# Equivalence checking as the golden test

When an agent proposes a new synthesis transformation, a script or a rule, the first question is never whether it improves QoR. It is whether it preserves function. Combinational equivalence checking answers that with a proof, so it is the golden test in any harness that lets models edit or extend a synthesis engine.

## A proof, not a sample

The harness runs every changed engine on a benchmark suite and checks each output network against its input with a miter and SAT. UNSAT on every benchmark means the transformation preserved function on those designs. Random simulation is not enough: it finds bugs quickly but cannot prove their absence, and synthesis bugs often live in rare corners. A satisfiable miter is a counterexample, a specific input on which the outputs differ. That is the most useful feedback the model can get, far better than a pass or fail bit, and it becomes a permanent regression test.

## Handling failures, timeouts and scope

One counterexample out of a hundred benchmarks proves a bug, so the change is rejected, not accepted at 99 percent. A timeout is not a pass: the change stays unproven until the check succeeds, for example by partitioning outputs, sweeping internal equivalences first, or using a stronger engine. Checking each transformation step separately gives small, fast miters and pinpoints the failing step, while an end-to-end check guards their composition. Combinational checking covers combinational passes only; a change that moves registers needs sequential equivalence, and one that uses environment don't cares must be checked modulo those constraints.

## Beyond correctness

Equivalence is necessary, not sufficient. A differential QoR check shows the change moves area and delay in the intended direction on the intended designs and nowhere else. Resource limits and determinism checks guard against run-time blowups and nondeterminism on unseen designs. The checker itself should be independent of the optimizer, built on a separate code path, so a shared bug cannot make both wrong in the same way. Together these make the harness loop safe: the model proposes, the tools verify, and a human reviews only changes that are already proven correct and shown useful.

## Going deeper

Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton and Een, "Improvements to combinational equivalence checking", ICCAD (2006); the golden and differential testing concept in this curriculum's agentic domain.

problems.q:
A miter is built for two versions of a circuit. When are they equivalent?

A) When the miter output is 1 on half the inputs

B) When the miter has fewer nodes than either circuit

C) When the miter output is satisfiable

D) When the miter output is unsatisfiable, that is, constant 0
problems.a: When the miter output is unsatisfiable, that is, constant 0
problems.e: The miter XORs corresponding outputs; any satisfying assignment is a counterexample.

problems.q:
Which transformation cannot be verified by combinational equivalence checking alone?

A) Balancing

B) Retiming, because registers move and lose their one-to-one correspondence

C) AIG rewriting

D) Technology mapping of combinational logic
problems.a: Retiming, because registers move and lose their one-to-one correspondence
problems.e: Sequential transformations need sequential equivalence checking.

problems.q:
Why is random simulation not enough as the golden test?

A) Simulation is slower than SAT on every circuit

B) It can miss rare differences; only a SAT or BDD proof covers every input vector

C) Simulation cannot handle AND gates

D) Simulation changes the circuit
problems.a: It can miss rare differences; only a SAT or BDD proof covers every input vector
problems.e: Simulation finds counterexamples quickly but cannot prove their absence.

problems.q:
An agent's transformation passes CEC on 99 benchmarks and fails on one. What should the harness do?

A) Reject it, feed the counterexample back to the model, and keep the failing design as a new golden test

B) Accept it, since 99% is good enough

C) Remove the failing benchmark from the suite

D) Accept it with a warning
problems.a: Reject it, feed the counterexample back to the model, and keep the failing design as a new golden test
problems.e: One counterexample proves a bug; the failing case becomes part of the regression.

problems.q:
Internal equivalences between the original and optimized AIG speed up CEC. Why?

A) Proving matched internal nodes first cuts the miter into small, easy SAT problems

B) They let CEC ignore primary outputs

C) They make the miter output constant 1

D) They remove the need for SAT entirely
problems.a: Proving matched internal nodes first cuts the miter into small, easy SAT problems
problems.e: SAT sweeping merges proven internal equivalences, so the output check becomes trivial.

problems.q:
CEC times out on a large design after an agent's change. What is a sound response?

A) Treat a timeout as a pass

B) Skip verification for large designs

C) Treat the result as unproven and do not promote the change until it is proved, for example with partitioning or FRAIG-based sweeping

D) Shorten the timeout until it passes
problems.a: Treat the result as unproven and do not promote the change until it is proved, for example with partitioning or FRAIG-based sweeping
problems.e: Absence of a counterexample within a time limit is not a proof.

problems.q:
Why should the equivalence checker belong to a different code path than the optimizer it checks?

A) Because optimizers cannot use SAT

B) A shared bug in a common component could make both the optimizer and the checker wrong in the same way

C) Because checkers must be slower

D) Because shared code cannot compile
problems.a: A shared bug in a common component could make both the optimizer and the checker wrong in the same way
problems.e: Independent verification avoids common-mode failures.

problems.q:
Beyond CEC, what does a differential QoR check add for an agent-proposed pass?

A) A proof of equivalence

B) Evidence that the pass moves area and delay in the intended direction on the intended designs and nowhere else

C) A new Liberty library

D) A faster SAT solver
problems.a: Evidence that the pass moves area and delay in the intended direction on the intended designs and nowhere else
problems.e: CEC proves correctness; differential QoR proves usefulness and absence of regressions.

problems.q:
Why should the equivalence checker belong to a different code path than the optimizer it checks?

A) Because checkers must be slower

B) A shared bug in a common component could make both the optimizer and the checker wrong in the same way

C) Because shared code cannot compile

D) Because optimizers cannot use SAT
problems.a: A shared bug in a common component could make both the optimizer and the checker wrong in the same way
problems.e: Independent verification avoids common-mode failures.

label: Fast versus accurate QoR in the loop
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast versus accurate QoR in the loop

An agent exploring synthesis recipes cannot run full mapping, placement and timing for every candidate. It scores most candidates with fast proxies, AIG node count, levels or a quick mapping, and spends accurate runs only where decisions are close. Knowing how proxies disagree with signoff metrics, and when to recurse to the accurate engine, is the core skill of a design-space exploration loop.

## Measuring proxy agreement

Compare the ranking a proxy gives with the ranking of the accurate metric. For four recipes, count the pairs ordered oppositely, the discordant pairs. With AIG node counts 963, 1046, 1115, 914 and mapped areas 480, 402, 433, 453, the pairs (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4) and (3, 4) are discordant: 4 of 6. Kendall's tau is (concordant minus discordant) over the number of pairs, here $(2 - 4)/6 = -1/3$. A proxy that disagrees this often should not choose the winner. Rank agreement over all pairs can be high while the top few are still misordered, which is exactly where the decision is made.

## Pruning with fast engines

A typical loop scores hundreds of candidates with fast metrics: AIG nodes for area, levels or a unit-delay LUT mapping for depth. It keeps a shortlist and runs full mapping and static timing only on that shortlist. The engine must expose cheap observation hooks after every pass, so the agent can read node count, level count and a quick mapped estimate without exporting the design. Learned surrogate estimators trained on mapped results can sharpen the fast scores, but an optimizer drives designs out of the training distribution, where the surrogate is least reliable, so periodic accurate checks are essential.

## When to recurse to accuracy

Escalate to the accurate engine when candidates differ by less than the proxy's error, when proxy and accurate rankings have disagreed on similar designs, or when the fast model omits something that matters here. Unit-delay depth ignores fanout load and wire delay, so a recipe that looks fast can be slow after real timing. Metric variance across seeds sets a noise floor: differences below it should not drive decisions. Reward functions built only on fast proxies invite reward hacking, so a loop's final choice always comes from accurate signoff-relevant metrics.

## Going deeper

The fast and accurate engine loop in this curriculum's agentic domain; Kendall, "A new measure of rank correlation", Biometrika (1938).

problems.q:
A synthesis loop scores recipes with a fast proxy (AIG node count) and occasionally runs mapping for the accurate metric (area). Results: recipe 1: 976 AIG nodes, 401 square microns of mapped area; recipe 2: 1116 AIG nodes, 479 square microns of mapped area; recipe 3: 950 AIG nodes, 461 square microns of mapped area; recipe 4: 1070 AIG nodes, 429 square microns of mapped area. Of the 6 pairs of recipes, how many does the proxy rank in the opposite order from the accurate metric?

A) 1

B) 3

C) 4

D) 2
problems.e: Compare every pair: 2 pairs are discordant. A loop trusting the proxy alone would pick a worse recipe whenever the best pair is discordant.

problems.q:
A synthesis loop scores recipes with a fast proxy (AIG node count) and occasionally runs mapping for the accurate metric (area). Results: recipe 1: 1112 AIG nodes, 451 square microns of mapped area; recipe 2: 962 AIG nodes, 478 square microns of mapped area; recipe 3: 942 AIG nodes, 441 square microns of mapped area; recipe 4: 1024 AIG nodes, 412 square microns of mapped area. Of the 6 pairs of recipes, how many does the proxy rank in the opposite order from the accurate metric?

A) 4

B) 2

C) 5

D) 3
problems.e: Compare every pair: 3 pairs are discordant. A loop trusting the proxy alone would pick a worse recipe whenever the best pair is discordant.

problems.q:
A synthesis loop scores recipes with a fast proxy (AIG node count) and occasionally runs mapping for the accurate metric (area). Results: recipe 1: 1032 AIG nodes, 451 square microns of mapped area; recipe 2: 949 AIG nodes, 478 square microns of mapped area; recipe 3: 998 AIG nodes, 416 square microns of mapped area; recipe 4: 1112 AIG nodes, 439 square microns of mapped area. Of the 6 pairs of recipes, how many does the proxy rank in the opposite order from the accurate metric?

A) 6

B) 5

C) 4

D) 3
problems.e: Compare every pair: 4 pairs are discordant. A loop trusting the proxy alone would pick a worse recipe whenever the best pair is discordant.

problems.q:
Which fast metric best tracks delay before mapping?

A) AIG level count, or the depth of a quick LUT or cell mapping

B) AIG node count alone

C) The number of commands in the script

D) Number of primary inputs
problems.a: AIG level count, or the depth of a quick LUT or cell mapping
problems.e: Level count measures logic depth; node count measures area.

problems.q:
A design-space exploration agent evaluates 500 recipes. Which plan uses fast and accurate engines well?

A) Pick a recipe at random, then run STA

B) Use only AIG node count and never map

C) Score all 500 with AIG metrics or a fast mapper, then run full mapping and STA on the top few

D) Run full place and route on all 500
problems.a: Score all 500 with AIG metrics or a fast mapper, then run full mapping and STA on the top few
problems.e: Fast proxies prune the space; accurate engines confirm the shortlist.

problems.q:
Which fast metric best tracks delay before mapping?

A) AIG level count, or the depth of a quick LUT or cell mapping

B) The number of commands in the script

C) Number of primary inputs

D) AIG node count alone
problems.a: AIG level count, or the depth of a quick LUT or cell mapping
problems.e: Level count measures logic depth; node count measures area.

problems.q:
The proxy and accurate metric agree on 90% of recipe pairs. Is the proxy safe to choose the final recipe?

A) Not by itself: the final choice is among the best candidates, exactly where small disagreements decide the winner

B) No, a proxy must agree on 100% of pairs to be useful

C) Yes, as long as node count decreased

D) Yes, 90% agreement guarantees the best recipe
problems.a: Not by itself: the final choice is among the best candidates, exactly where small disagreements decide the winner
problems.e: Rank correlation over all pairs can be high while the top-k ordering is still wrong.

problems.q:
How should the variance of a fast metric across seeds influence the loop?

A) The loop should pick the recipe with the highest variance

B) High variance means the proxy is accurate

C) Variance is irrelevant if the mean is good

D) High variance means differences below the noise floor should not drive decisions without accurate confirmation
problems.a: High variance means differences below the noise floor should not drive decisions without accurate confirmation
problems.e: Decisions are only as reliable as the metric's resolution.

problems.q:
The proxy and accurate metric agree on 90% of recipe pairs. Is the proxy safe to choose the final recipe?

A) Yes, as long as node count decreased

B) No, a proxy must agree on 100% of pairs to be useful

C) Yes, 90% agreement guarantees the best recipe

D) Not by itself: the final choice is among the best candidates, exactly where small disagreements decide the winner
problems.a: Not by itself: the final choice is among the best candidates, exactly where small disagreements decide the winner
problems.e: Rank correlation over all pairs can be high while the top-k ordering is still wrong.

label: Change tiers for a synthesis engine
lesson:
# Change tiers for a synthesis engine

A synthesis engine fits the four-layer model cleanly. The AIG with structural hashing and the contract that every pass preserves function is the core. Scripts and pass selection are strategy, numbers such as cut size and iteration counts are parameters, and per-pass statistics are observation hooks. Classifying a customer request into the smallest safe tier is the first decision of an agentic change loop.

## The layers of a synthesis engine

The immutable core is the AIG data structure, structural hashing, the transformation contract (every pass preserves function) and the equivalence checker. Strategy is the choice and order of passes, the recipe, plus pluggable policies such as which cones to balance. Parameters are numbers: cut size, number of rewriting iterations, whether to accept zero-gain moves, level preservation. Observation hooks report node count, levels and estimated mapped QoR after each pass. A request to use 6-input cuts instead of 4-input cuts in rewriting is Tier 1 if the core supports it; a request to make AIG nodes carry a new attribute through every pass is Tier 3.

## Seams for customer-specific behavior

The behavior that varies most between customers is the cost judgment inside passes: whether a replacement is better. The right seam is a cost provider that the rewriter calls for each candidate replacement, given the cut, MFFC size, the candidate's node count and levels, and the node's timing criticality. A customer who penalizes XOR-heavy structures, or who weights depth on critical cones only, then writes a Tier 2 plug-in. The seam should be called per batch of candidates, not per node visit, so the core's hot loops stay inlined. FSM encoding heuristics and rule sets for datapath rewriting are similar Tier 2 extension points.

## Proof and promotion

A Tier 2 plug-in passes the golden tests (equivalence on every benchmark) and a differential QoR test showing that results changed only on designs where the new cost should matter, by the intended amount. Tier 3 changes, even pure speedups of the hash table, need a human-reviewed diff and full regression, because every pass depends on the core. If customer requests keep landing in Tier 3, the seam is in the wrong place. A recipe or plug-in that works for one customer is validated, promoted into the library with guidance on when to select it, and the customer's design stays private.

## Going deeper

The four-layer engine model and change tiers in this curriculum's agentic domain; Brayton and Mishchenko, "ABC: an academic industrial-strength verification tool", CAV (2010).

problems.q:
A customer asks for a recipe that runs balance only on timing-critical cones. Which tier?

A) Tier 1: a flag of balance

B) Tier 3: rewriting the AIG data structure

C) Tier 2: a new strategy plug-in that selects cones using a timing hook and calls the existing balance pass

D) Tier 1: changing the Liberty library
problems.a: Tier 2: a new strategy plug-in that selects cones using a timing hook and calls the existing balance pass
problems.e: It composes existing transformations under a new policy at an extension point.

problems.q:
In the four-layer model for a synthesis engine, what is the immutable core?

A) The list of designs in the benchmark suite

B) The default resyn2 script

C) The AIG data structure with structural hashing and the equivalence-preserving transformation contract

D) The cut size and iteration counts
problems.a: The AIG data structure with structural hashing and the equivalence-preserving transformation contract
problems.e: Scripts are policy and numbers are parameters; the representation and its invariants are the core.

problems.q:
A customer asks the synthesis engine to use 6-input cuts instead of 4-input cuts in rewriting. Which tier?

A) Tier 3: a change to the AIG core

B) Tier 2: a new rewriting plug-in

C) Tier 1: a parameter of the rewriting skill

D) Not an engine change at all
problems.a: Tier 1: a parameter of the rewriting skill
problems.e: Cut size is a parameter, as long as the core supports it; no new code is needed.

problems.q:
A customer wants their own FSM encoding heuristic. Where does it belong?

A) A Tier 3 edit to the AIG

B) A Tier 2 encoder plug-in at the FSM pass's encoding extension point

C) A Tier 1 flag of ABC's strash

D) A change to the Liberty library
problems.a: A Tier 2 encoder plug-in at the FSM pass's encoding extension point
problems.e: Encoding is a policy choice inside a pass with a stable interface.

problems.q:
What context should a rewriting cost seam expose?

A) The customer's revenue target

B) The cut, the MFFC size, the candidate's node count and levels, and the node's timing criticality

C) Only the node's name

D) The full RTL source
problems.a: The cut, the MFFC size, the candidate's node count and levels, and the node's timing criticality
problems.e: A cost decision needs local structure and live observations, nothing else.

problems.q:
Why should a cost seam be called per candidate batch rather than per AND node visit?

A) Batches change the function

B) Coarse calls let the core keep its hot loops inlined and fast

C) Per-node calls are not deterministic

D) The core cannot call plug-ins
problems.a: Coarse calls let the core keep its hot loops inlined and fast
problems.e: Seam granularity matters for performance; fine-grained virtual calls in the hot loop are expensive.

problems.q:
A plug-in rewriting cost passes golden CEC tests. What else must the differential test show?

A) That the core code changed

B) That QoR changed only on designs where the new cost should matter, by the intended amount

C) That run time doubled

D) That every design got smaller
problems.a: That QoR changed only on designs where the new cost should matter, by the intended amount
problems.e: Differential evidence shows the plug-in did what it claimed and nothing else.

problems.q:
The harness reports that a requested change needs a Tier 3 edit every time a customer asks for a new cost. What does that say?

A) Tier 3 edits are the normal path

B) The golden tests are too strict

C) The seam is in the wrong place: cost should be an extension point, not part of the core

D) The customers are asking for too much
problems.a: The seam is in the wrong place: cost should be an extension point, not part of the core
problems.e: A well-placed seam makes common requests Tier 1 or Tier 2.

problems.q:
A recipe found for one customer works well on similar designs. What is the flywheel path?

A) Delete it after the project

B) Hard-code it as the new default for everyone immediately

C) Ship the customer's design with it

D) Validate it with golden and differential tests, promote it into the recipe library, and record when to select it
problems.a: Validate it with golden and differential tests, promote it into the recipe library, and record when to select it
problems.e: Validated know-how is promoted with selection guidance; design data stays private.
